#4610. Losing even one hour of sleep can make you more susceptible to scams

Published Nov 9, 2026 3:00 PM EST

A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health. New evidence indicates that losing as little as one hour of rest may increase your chance of falling for an online scam by over 10 percent the following morning. Neurobiologists at the University of California, Irvine, laid out their findings in a study published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), arguing that even minimal sleep disruptions can have almost immediate consequences.

“Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” said UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.

If you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone. Cybercrimes continue to increase exponentially in the United States. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million reports in 2025—a nearly 25 percent increase from only five years earlier.

Remaining aware of con artist tactics and staying up-to-date on personal cybersecurity strategies are some of the best ways to protect yourself. However, Schechtman and his colleagues recently wondered if something as seemingly inconsequential as a single evening of bad sleep may also put people at risk for schemes like an email phishing attack. To investigate, the team partnered with a large, unnamed company as it ran a cybersecurity awareness campaign for more than 11,000 employees. Multiple times a year, the company’s IT department issued emails imitating phishing attempts, then tallied how many workers clicked through the fake malicious links. Schechtman’s team then analyzed results both before the switch to Daylight Saving Time (DST), as well as the Monday after employees lost an hour of sleep.

On the Monday prior to DST, workers clicked on a phishing email link about 15.5 percent. of the time. Then, the Monday immediately following DST saw that rate rise to about 17.7 percent. That may not seem like much, but the difference comes out to about a 13 percent increase in phishing victims after losing approximately just one hour of sleep. According to Schechtman, there are multiple ways to contextualize these results.

“First, they give us a peek into the effects of very minor sleep loss… [from] Daylight Saving Time, which is similar in scope to the kind of sleep loss that many of us experience daily,” he said. “Although we focused on cybersecurity, many of our day-to-day decisions are likely compromised in similar ways.”

Schechtman hopes both employers and cybersecurity companies take regularly sleep-depriving events like DST, holidays, and even primetime sporting events into consideration when advising the public on phishing awareness. In the meantime, he stressed that even those who regularly suffer from sleep issues continue to prioritize their rest as much as possible.

“Better sleep likely leads to better decisions,” he added.

#4609. Hyundai Facing Class-Action Lawsuit Over Driver Monitoring System's Alleged False Alarms

According to the lawsuit, Hyundai knew its driver monitoring cameras had issues, but suggested drivers try fixes like different eyeglasses.

Automakers are constantly striving to make cars safer. New technologies such as automatic emergency braking, lane-keep assist, and driver monitoring systems were all developed to prevent crashes. However, according to a recent class-action lawsuit, one of those technologies designed to keep us out of trouble may be causing more trouble than it’s worth.

According to ClassAction.org, a 70-page complaint filed September 16 in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California alleges that Hyundai's Direct Driver Monitoring System (DDMS) in the 2024-2026 Hyundai Santa Fe, 2025-2026 Ioniq 5, 2025-2026 Tucson, 2025-2026 Santa Cruz, and 2026 Palisade incorrectly identifies attentive drivers as distracted. The plaintiffs argue that this goes far beyond simple annoying warning messages, as the vehicles could also disable the cruise control system and even trigger unexpected automatic braking.

The logic behind Hyundai's DDMS is sound. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 315,167 people were injured by distracted driving in 2024 alone. Hyundai is attempting to reduce this number by using their DDMS to check for signs of distracted driving, with the setup working with the Forward Attention Warning (FAW) system to monitor the driver’s eyes, face and head position using a camera. When it detects what it believes to be distracted driving, it will alert the driver; if the system repeatedly detects an inattentive driver while cruise control is engaged, it can deactivate cruise control and initiate an emergency stop, bringing the vehicle to a halt.

But several Hyundai owners claim the DDMS is flagging drivers who are fully alert and paying attention to the road. According to the plaintiffs in this case, Hyundai knew about this potential flaw nearly two years ago when the company issued technical service bulletin 25-GI-001H in January 2025. According to the lawsuit, Hyundai’s proposed solution to the problem was that drivers “need to wear different sunglasses or glasses, adjust their seats, and look at the road.”

The lawsuit states that Hyundai's own owner's manuals acknowledge that its driver monitoring system may malfunction under a surprisingly wide range of normal driving conditions: wearing sunglasses, prescription glasses, heavy makeup, or a hat can interfere with the camera; so can bright sunlight, laughing, squinting, turning your head, or simply being too tall or too short. Even a bumpy road or the position of your hands on the steering wheel can reportedly confuse the system. (In other words, quite a few things people routinely do while driving could potentially trigger false warnings.)

The lawsuit seeks damages and other relief for affected Hyundai owners, but the allegations have yet to be proven in court.

#4607. Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

Published Nov 9, 2026 3:00 PM EST

The old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) likely watch adults making different vocalization to learn how and when to use those sounds themselves, particularly when they purse their lips to blow “raspberries.” The findings detailed in a study published today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) show that the primates’ sounds are not instinctual and set in stone, as previously believed.

Humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing. For example, English speakers mimic dogs with “woof,” while French speakers say “ouaf.” When it comes to our primate relatives, biologists generally used to believe that they didn’t learn sounds from one another, and that instead biology dictated their sounds. However, that’s changing with some new research into two groups of Chimpanzees in a couple of west African countries.

To probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry. Chimpanzees make this unvoiced sound that’s similar to how humans push their lips together to blow raspberries. The team looked at how 91 chimpanzees, from birth to 55 years old, used the raspberry call. They studied a group of wild chimpanzees from four communities in Taï National Park, Ivory Coast, and a group of young, orphaned, and peer-raised chimpanzees at Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Sierra Leone.

The team found that the wild Ivory Coast chimpanzees almost exclusively used the raspberry while grooming others. However, the juveniles at the Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary used it across a much wider range of social situations.

If blowing a raspberry is only an instinctive call, the groups should be using it in similar ways no matter where they were raised. According to the team, these differences suggest that chimpanzees learn from adults how to make a call, as well as when and why to use it.

“In everyday communication, we use the words that we do only because our peers do too. It’s communal practice that fixes their meaning, rather than features of the words themselves,” Richard Moore, a study co-author and mind, language, and psychology philosopher at the University of Warwick, said in a statement.

“The discovery that this is true not just for natural languages but also some chimpanzee calls means there’s more continuity between chimpanzees’ vocal learning and our own than we previously suspected.”

The team also say that when an adult chimpanzee was introduced to one of the groups living in the Tacugama sanctuary, the young chimps gradually began to use the raspberry more consistently and began to resemble the adult’s noises. This suggests that adults serve as role models, helping a community settle in on shared communication patterns.

The researchers say this is the first time that this kind of learned and agreed-upon sound use has been shown in chimpanzee calls. The link between the raspberry sound and its use appears to be shared from one chimpanzee to another, and is not built in at birth. While chimpanzees struggle to learn entirely new call sounds, the study suggests that they can learn the meaning behind sounds that they already know how to make but didn’t use in the same way as other chimps.

“Even aspects of chimpanzee vocal communication that seemed fixed and unlearned may be shaped by learning, suggesting that there is still much to discover about their vocal repertoire,”

added Antoine Valet, a study co-author and cognitive scientist at the Institute of Cognitive Sciences (CNRS) in France.

Additionally, the team has some theories on why different chimpanzee populations use the raspberry in similar ways if it is a learned sound.

“One possibility is that, whilst grooming, as chimpanzees use their lips to extract parasites from another’s fur, it may be easier to generate a vocalisation that uses similar lip movements, a call that is known to prolong grooming bouts,” explained study co-author and CNRS behavioral ecologist Catherine Crockford. “Communities may have found this useful independently, but that wouldn’t change the fact that the call is a convention. We need more research to test it.”

#4606. The Yangwang Altior is a Mega-Luxury Electric Sedan from China Aimed Right at Rolls-Royce

BYD’s luxury arm has an answer to those in the super-luxury end of the market with this quad-motor EV. It even looks like a Rolls.

Last week, Yangwang broke a speed record. This week, the Chinese luxury car brand is doing something rather different: it’s revealing a Rolls-Royce-esque full-size luxury sedan called the Altior. And sure, plenty of the details are unique to this Yangwang, but it’s hard to look at this sedan and not see the famous Ghost in its proportions (it’s about two inches longer than one) and design language.

The chassis and powertrain under this car’s sheet metal is nothing like that of the Rolls it looks so much like, though. Instead of a V-12, the Altior is fitted with a quad-motor electric powertrain, with all four electric motors independent from one another. Total output isn’t available, but we suspect it will have to be somewhere in the 1000-horsepower range with that many electric motors.

Yangwang makes several neat claims as to the car’s abilities. For one, it’s apparently capable of performing a tank turn; we’re not sure how useful that will be in a luxury sedan, but the possibility exists. An active body control system reads the road ahead and adjusts the suspension to provide the most comfortable ride possible. Yangwang also claims the Altior has an “emergency flotation capability” that can “provide additional support if the vehicle accidentally enters water.” That sounds similar to Elon Musk’s claims about the Cybertruck being capable of briefly acting as a boat ... and in both cases, we wouldn’t recommend testing the claim.

Power comes from what Yangwang says is its second-generation “Blade Battery,” and the claim is 621 miles of range on China’s very optimistic CLTC cycle. Charging specs weren’t revealed, but the Blade Battery 2.0 with “Flash Charging” (which the Altior has) in the Yangwang U7 has an astounding peak charging rate of about 1500 kilowatts.

The Altior’s interior is undeniably gorgeous, though it trades much of the ornamentation of a Rolls for the tech-forward screens we’re accustomed to seeing in high-end Chinese EVs. Hetian jade is used for the air vents, while semi-aniline leather is found on the seats, and Yangwang uses Suzhou embroidery (the technique involves splitting silk threads) to create flowing cloud motifs. Real metal switches are found throughout. The floor mats are made of wool, and natural woods were selected for the trim.

A four-seat layout and so-called zero-gravity seats with massage ensure the rear occupants are mighty comfortable. The car has a 39-speaker Dynaudio sound system, while a 21.4-inch overhead screen drops down to provide entertainment for those in the back. Plus, there are two fridges, and the one in the rear even has a warming function. In case you needed further evidence of the inspiration Rolls had on this interior’s design, there are even bespoke umbrellas that are integrated in the doors. (That said, Yangwang says it got the idea from the “Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests at China’s Temple of Heaven complex,” with no mention of Rolls to be found.)

This massive sedan sure won’t see roads in the U.S., but Yangwang intends to sell it in Europe in the future, where it can go toe-to-toe with the British-made luxury sedans it borrows so much from.

#4605. Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of new technologies.”

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

The campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

“Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is important for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

“A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he said it was also fulfilling.

“I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he said.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar said. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”

As he embraces his 50s, he said he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

He also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

“[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar said.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”

#4604. Yamaha’s new electric scooter takes aim at Europe’s 125cc commuters

Yamaha is expanding its electric scooter lineup with the new XENTER E, a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter designed specifically with European city riding in mind.

Unveiled around EICMA 2026 in Milan alongside the new NMAX E, the XENTER E is a high-wheel scooter riding on 16-inch wheels front and rear.

That’s an important distinction in European cities, where larger wheels can make quick work of the cobblestones, potholes, and tram tracks that can turn smaller-wheeled scooters into teeth-rattling experiences.

The XENTER E uses Yamaha’s new eAxle powertrain, combining the motor, controller, and reduction gearbox into a compact frame-mounted unit. The motor produces 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power and 33.3 Nm of torque, putting the scooter into Europe’s A1 license category.

Mounting the motor to the frame also means Yamaha can use a more conventional motorcycle-style swingarm rather than hanging the motor on the rear suspension like many scooters. That reduces unsprung weight and should help improve handling and ride quality.

Power is supplied from an integrated 3.5 kWh battery mounted low in the chassis. Yamaha claims 108 km (67 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 cycle, though real-world range is expected to be somewhat lower.

An 800W onboard charger can refill the battery in around 5.5 hours from a public charging station. Yamaha will also offer a cable for charging from a household outlet.

Other niceties include three riding modes, traction control, regenerative braking, a reverse mode for maneuvering at low speeds, smart-key operation, and a 5-inch TFT display. Smartphone connectivity adds navigation, battery information, maintenance reminders, and parking-location tracking.

For about four days now, I am thinking this could be my next ride. A 4 or 4,5 Kwh battery would be a real nice. But for now, it fits perfectly in my daily commute and I could trade in my 2024 Honda supercub. However, € 7800 is too much.. for this kind of money, or just a tad more, there are several low mileage BMW's CE04 on the market.

There’s also enough underseat storage for a full-face helmet, depending on its size, plus USB-C charging and provisions for accessories such as a windscreen and 34-liter top case.

The XENTER E shares its powertrain and battery with Yamaha’s new NMAX E, but the high-wheel layout gives it a distinctly more European commuter flavor.

Yamaha hasn’t officially announced pricing for each market, though early reports from Milan point to €7,799 in Germany. Deliveries are expected to begin in spring 2027.

It’s certainly not cheap, but the XENTER E looks like Yamaha is finally getting serious about building electric scooters that can replace its bread-and-butter 125cc urban machines, rather than simply supplement them.

#4603. Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:00 PM EST

Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes. Prehistoric cultures unfortunately didn’t have this luxury, and often responded dramatically to such changes. In northern Peru, archaeological evidence indicates local societies sometimes even turned to mass human sacrifices in an attempt to stop destructive flooding from events like El Niño.

That said, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate issues. According to their study recently published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, such brutal moments were actually pretty rare occurrences in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley.

“The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” said New York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.

The Lambayeque Valley is located inside northern Peru’s coastal desert, but the region has hosted residents for  6,000 years. Although the valley generally receives little rainfall, its rivers and proximity to the sea allowed communities to flourish there for generations, including societies like the Moche from roughly 100–750 CE, and the Sicán from about 750–1375 CE.

“Archaeological evidence shows that in so many ways they were mirrors of us—in how they lived their daily lives, interacted with their world, ran their economies, and confronted (and sometimes contributed to) environmental crises,” explained George Mason University archaeologist and study co-author Haagen Klaus.

Previous excavations have indicated that mass human sacrifices possibly preceded the collapse of the Moche and Sicán’s political systems. Researchers have since hypothesized that these acts likely coincided with periods of mass flooding,probably due to El Niño weather oscillations. Just like today, these weather events destroyed food stocks and disrupted agricultural production. Since large human sacrificial rituals may have been attempts by the ruling class to restore balance to nature, the team to wonder if violence was simply a more common facet of everyday life for the Moche and Sicán.

“If these big ritual sacrifices were indicative of some underlying crisis, we hypothesized that these events might have been extending into people’s everyday experience of the world,” said Snyder.

Klaus, Snyder, and their collaborators turned to the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project’s skeletal archive for answers. The collection spans about 3,000 years of history across 30 different archaeological sites. The team established relatively precise death estimates for over 1,600 individuals, while also examining them for evidence of intentional cranial trauma associated with human sacrifice. Contrary to their theory, only 25 remains (1.6 percent of the sample pool) showed signs of violence, while just 77 displayed indicators of accidental trauma. Of those, none were directly linked to known periods of past ecological crises.

“In Lambayeque, there’s 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and longer-term changes in climate, and widespread violence wasn’t one of them,” concluded Klaus.

The study’s authors noted that because they were notable to radiocarbon date all of the remains, their findings remain broader estimates of wide time periods. At the same time, they stressed the evidence underscores humanity’s history of facing intense climate challenges not with violence, but adaptation.

“This really highlights that widespread violence isn’t a predetermined response to climate change,” said Snyder. “As a society, we both get to and have to choose how we respond to our own climate crisis.”

“Violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes, ever,” added Klaus.

#4602. Police Say BMW M5 Street Racer Hid His Face and Plates, But Couldn't Hide His Identity Forever

Authorities identified an allegedly masked BMW driver and arrested him at a Brampton, Ontario home after a three-month investigation.

It's no big secret that some folks treat driving laws like they're optional. To avoid getting busted for such behavior, some obscure their plates; others try to mask their face. One kid who allegedly did both around Toronto, Ontario is now facing serious charges because police still managed to track him down over the course of three months—and took his BMW away, to top things off.

Police in the Ontario region of Peel say they started tracking the suspect in August. On the 30th of that month, officers say they saw the driver of a red BMW M5 participating in a street race at 1:06 in the morning. It's unclear if they gave chase, but either way, they didn't catch the driver that day. Around a month later, police say they saw the car again; on September 26, it popped up at two different street racing locations as a participant, and the driver allegedly ran a red light in view of police. While they didn't snag the driver on that occasion, it appears authorities leveraged traffic cameras to start making a case. The driver was allegedly wearing a ski mask for much of his antics, and reportedly drove without a license plate.

A red BMW M sedan isn't exactly subtle or super-common. So, after a few months of investigation, police obtained a warrant and arrested Tarman Toor, a 24-year-old living in Brampton, and charged him with three counts each of dangerous operation, disguise with intent, and racing a motor vehicle. It's unclear if he's still in jail as of this story’s publication, but police say he has a meeting with a judge on the schedule in the near future.

Peel Regional Police say they they've arrested 119 people for traffic violations this year, and charged 214 with stunt driving in their area alone. Each one of those comes with a 14-day impound of the car in question and a 30-day license suspension for the driver. If convicted, Toor could face worse: several years in jail over just one of these charges, much less all nine of them.

#4601. Harbinger scores another $240M in latest investment round

Electric truck maker Harbinger has been racking up wins in recent months, and after scoring a $300 million order from international shipping giant FedEx and a defense contract with the US military, the company has drummed up another $240 million in Series D funding.

Companies like FedEx and Amazon have been making serious moves to fully electrify their fleet operations, both in an effort to decarbonize and to avoid the every-increasing price of diesel. At $300 million for 2,000 medium-duty electric delivery trucks, Harbinger’s latest deal with FedEx is believed to be one of the largest binding orders for electric medium or heavy-duty trucks in history – and it’s a big enough deal to inspire more than 240 million votes of confidence in the company’s future, one dollar at a time.

“Harbinger exists to challenge what industry has learned to accept, and reinvent the critical systems the world depends on,” said John Harris, the Co-Founder and CEO of Harbinger. “By rethinking critical systems from first principles, we aim to unlock better performance, greater reliability, safer operations, and more room to grow. Electrification is at the core of everything we do, and increasingly, electrification is at the core of industry, defense, mobility, and AI. Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option. It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

Harbinger’s Series D funding round was co-led by Tiger Global, the Capricorn Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline. The company says the new funding will support expansion into energy storage systems, power generation, autonomy software, and defense applications, as well as the continued ramp up of its medium-duty platform manufacturing capacity. With this latest round of financing, Harbinger has raised over $650 million since 2021.

As for me, I’m hoping they use the money to come up with more fun, high-octane chase videos that show off their trucks’ performance capabilities. Time will tell.

#4599. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” said Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel said in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel said in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.

#4598. Tesla deemed liable for fraud after Solar Roof ‘experiment’ on a home

A California judge has deemed Tesla liable for fraud in a Solar Roof lawsuit, after the company repeatedly failed to hand over evidence. Tesla had already admitted it breached the contract, broke its warranty, and was negligent on the job.

The homeowner says fixing the damage will cost “well over $2.5 million.” Tesla once offered him $5,000.

The case is Conroy v. Tesla, filed in 2022 in San Diego Superior Court’s North County division (case No. 37-2022-00043670). Electrek reviewed the court orders, the complaint, and the parties’ joint trial readiness report. Here’s what’s in them.

Ambrose Conroy, who lives in Rancho Santa Fe, signed up for a Tesla Solar Roof in March 2020. The original contract was $82,210 for a 13.1 kW system. By February 2021, after two amendments, it had grown to roughly $110,000 for an 18.2 kW roof and six Powerwalls.

The roof was never finished. It never passed a county inspection, and it never produced a single kWh for the house.

Tesla isn’t contesting most of that anymore. In the joint report filed by both sides last month, Tesla stipulated to liability on three of the five claims.

The other two claims, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, are where things went badly for Tesla.

Judge Cynthia Freeland sanctioned Tesla twice over discovery before going further. She ordered it to pay $15,467.50 in February and another $13,500 in June, both times for failing to produce a proper privilege log and responsive documents, and both times warning that issue sanctions could follow.

Tesla missed the next deadline anyway. So on September 11, the court deemed Tesla liable for fraud and negligent misrepresentation, limiting the trial on those claims to compensatory and punitive damages.

The judge found “ample evidence to support that Defendants have acted willfully.” Among the missing records were Microsoft Teams messages (Tesla’s own corporate witness testified they’re kept “for infinity”), OSHA logs, emails with San Diego County inspectors, and more than 20 quality, install, and safety reports from Tesla’s internal Bolt system.

Tesla asked her to reconsider, arguing it had since produced everything. She said no in a ruling dated October 27, writing that the late documents could support Conroy’s theory that Tesla “knowingly used Plaintiff’s home as an experiment while knowing they lacked the experience to perform as promised.”

And the “experiment” word shows up in Tesla’s own messages, according to the trial exhibit list. Exhibit 224 is described as text messages from January 13, 2021, between Tesla’s director of model engineering Bobby Yang and other Tesla employees.

To be clear, that’s how Conroy’s side describes the messages on the exhibit list. We haven’t seen the texts themselves. But Elon Musk is on Conroy’s witness list, and internal emails quoted in the complaint point the same way.

On February 9, 2021, Yang wrote internally that the house was in the “99.5 percentile in terms of complexity” and that “if we can do this job well, we should be able to do any job well.” RJ Johnson, then head of Tesla’s energy business, replied that the project would “skew numbers” but that Tesla needed “to make it right.”

Johnson was fired in April 2021. The roof had at least 59 mounting planes, and one employee called it the largest job Tesla had attempted at the time, according to the complaint.

Conroy’s account of the installation reads like a list of everything that can go wrong on a roof. These are his allegations, but Tesla has now conceded breach and negligence.

The tear-off was supposed to take two days and took two weeks. Tesla left in November 2020 with bare roof decking exposed, then had crews work overtime on December 27 to get underlayment down before a storm. Tiles arrived scratched and damaged and went on the roof anyway. Glass tiles shattered in the driveway and lawn, and the family says they still can’t walk there barefoot.

By March 2021, Johnson had agreed in writing that paying “when you’re happy with the outcome is completely reasonable.” Tesla’s billing department kept calling anyway.

In August 2021, an internal email weighed just leaving.

The project went through at least seven project managers. In November 2021, Tesla told Conroy the people behind its repair plan were gone and it had nobody in the area to do the work.

In April 2022, Tesla offered $5,000 to settle everything.

It didn’t end there. In February 2025, more than two years into the lawsuit, Tesla failed another San Diego County inspection after showing up without the plans for the venting system. And this summer, Conroy’s electrical expert opened up part of the roof and concluded that the way Tesla ran wiring and conduit under the tiles created a short-circuit and fire risk in heavy rain. The roof is now coming off. Tesla’s lawyers point out that even Conroy’s counsel called that fire risk “counterintuitive.”

Tesla is fighting the sanction hard. In an October 29 filing, it asked the court to freeze the case while it petitions the California Court of Appeal, arguing the order is “unduly punitive,” violates due process, and amounts to a directed verdict on fraud before trial.

Tesla also says the discovery fight had no connection to the fraud claims and that it has now produced everything relevant. The judge already rejected that argument once.

The November 20 trial date is off. A trial readiness conference is set for December 4, and Conroy’s lawyers want to go to trial in December.

This isn’t the first Solar Roof horror story in this case file. Conroy’s complaint attaches our 2020 report on a Solar Roof buyer left with tarps over his house after Tesla tried an untested underlayment on his home. It also cites a 2025 California Contractors State License Board action seeking to revoke Tesla’s contractor licenses over abandoned Solar Roof jobs.

What a nightmare. This is the most damaging Solar Roof case I’ve seen, and I’ve been covering this product since Elon Musk unveiled it on a Universal Studios backlot in 2016.

A botched install isn’t news on its own. Tesla only installed about 3,000 of these roofs before killing the product this year, and plenty of them went sideways. What’s different here is the paper trail: internal emails calling a customer’s home a test of whether Tesla could do “any job,” texts describing the job as an “experiment” with daily reports going to Musk, and then years of Tesla failing to hand over its own records until a judge ran out of patience.

And Tesla’s response to all of it was $5,000.

Look, it’s normal for things not to go as planned with a new product, and early adopters need to be flexible. However, we are talking about someone’s literal roof over their head here and a trillion-dollar company. Tesla could have and should have made it right a long time ago.

Any time there are internal messages in the record that say essentially "let's skip town rather than try to make this right", it's a tough lift to make a jury think that everything was aboveboard.

The question that strikes me is whether this may also rise to the criminal level, since the CEO was apparently involved in the decision.

The issue sanction might not survive the Court of Appeal. Courts don’t love deciding fraud through discovery orders, and Tesla’s due process argument isn’t frivolous. But even if it gets reversed, Tesla has still admitted it breached the contract and was negligent, and the jury will see how this customer was treated.

This also says a lot about how Tesla ran the Solar Roof business. It sold a product it knew was hard to install, on homes it knew were complex, while the people running the program kept leaving. Conroy’s house was one of the worst cases, but installers are still dealing with the fallout of Tesla walking away from the product earlier this year.

The real question is what’s in those Teams messages and texts Tesla fought so hard to keep out of this case. If this goes to trial in December, we might find out.

#4596. BYD Offices Raided in Legal Probe Over Land Rover Defender Similarities

The BYD Ti7 bears more than a passing resemblance to Land Rover’s current off-road champ, but is that enough to make a case in court?

American buyers may not be familiar with the BYD Ti 7, a Chinese-made three-row hybrid SUV with a boxy shape and an unusual square of painted surface floating above the beltline. They will, however, be familiar with the Land Rover Defender sold in the U.S., a three-row SUV with a boxy shape and an unusual square of painted surface floating above the beltline. And according to a report from British newspaper The Times, Land Rover may have noticed some similarities between the two SUVs.

Last August, according to The Times, a court-ordered raid of BYD’s Dutch offices occurred on behalf of Land Rover company JLR. This was, reportedly, to find documents surrounding how a Land Rover Defender was used in the Ti 7’s development—evidence that could be key in a potential legal case over similarities between the models.

The BYD Ti 7 starts at the equivalent of $27,000 below the MSRP of the most affordable three-row Defenders on the U.K market. It also gets a plug-in hybrid powertrain alongside its seven-seat layout, while Land Rover’s plug-in Defender is only available in England with six seats.

Notably, Land Rover has already been involved in one lawsuit over another automaker attempting to build a product that looks astonishingly similar to a Defender. That model, the Ineos Grenadier, was cleared for sale in 2020 despite looking, well, much like an original Defender.

In the case of the BYD Ti 7, the visual similarities with Land Rover’s larger Defenders are obvious. The question is how much the two SUVs actually have in common, and whether or not it is enough to build a winning legal argument. Top Gear reports that a Dutch court will decide whether a case will proceed later this week.

#4595. Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles

If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.

Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.

Because while the West keeps trying to electrify pickup trucks and SUVs, much of the world has already settled on a far more sensible transportation appliance.

Western readers often think of a sedan as the world’s “normal” or “sensible” vehicle.

But go traveling almost anywhere in Asia, and that illusion disappears in about five minutes.

The roads are filled with Honda Clicks and CG125s, Hero Splendors, Yamaha NMAXs and YBR125s, and countless other small-displacement motorcycles. They carry workers to jobs, students to school, families to dinner, and every imaginable cargo in between.

They’re the delivery vans. They’re the commuter cars. They’re grocery getters, family transportation, and work trucks. And perhaps more importantly, they transport hundreds of millions of people every single day.

You don’t have to spend long in places like the Philippines before realizing something else: these aren’t really “motorcycle cultures.” They’re just transportation cultures. People ride these machines because they make sense.

And I’ve done it myself to see what all the fuss was about. Sure, I’m an e-motorcycle guy through and through. But I’ve been there to ride a mile in their motorcycle sandals, and so I get it.

Even so, having had one cheek on each saddle, I still have to think there’s a better way than the tried-and-true 125cc combustion engine motorcycles that have become the workhorse of much of the world.

The extreme proliferation of small motorcycles is what makes the current electric motorcycle market feel so strange. If there were ever a class of gasoline vehicle that batteries are already capable of replacing, it’s the 125cc combustion engine motorcycle.

These bikes aren’t demanding. They generally produce a modest 10-15 hp (8–11 kW) of power. They cruise comfortably around 45-60 mph (70-100 km/h). Most riders travel relatively short daily distances measured in dozens of miles, not hundreds.

A modern electric motorcycle with a 4-6 kWh battery can comfortably accomplish those same tasks while offering smoother acceleration, quieter operation, lower maintenance, and dramatically lower operating costs.

Unlike replacing a heavy-duty pickup truck that tows livestock trailers across Montana, replacing a 125cc commuter bike is already well within today’s battery technology. In many ways, it’s one of the easiest transportation sectors to electrify.

Instead, North America’s electric motorcycle market developed in an odd direction.

We have electric bicycles, and those are great for urban commuters. But then we jump almost straight to premium electric motorcycles costing $15,000 to $25,000. The practical middle has remained surprisingly sparse.

The ONYX RCR became something of a cult favorite by proving there was genuine demand for lightweight, motorcycle-like electric transportation without superbike performance.

Ryvid’s Anthem pushed further, adding highway capability while still remaining approachable and relatively affordable.

The new LiveWire S4 Honcho also feels like an encouraging step toward a lighter, more practical electric motorcycle instead of another oversized premium machine.

Even Infinite Machine’s Olto, while occupying a slightly different category, demonstrates growing interest in practical urban electric two-wheelers that prioritize transportation over headline horsepower.

These companies are proving something important: People don’t necessarily need 100 horsepower. Many simply need transportation.

Don’t misunderstand me. Electric pickup trucks absolutely have their place. Electric SUVs do too.

But we’ve spent the last decade pouring enormous engineering effort into electrifying some of the least energy-efficient passenger vehicles on the road.

Meanwhile, we’ve largely ignored one of the most efficient gasoline vehicle classes humanity has ever created.

A typical 125cc combustion engine motorcycle can already achieve fuel economy approaching or exceeding 100 mpg (2.35 liters/100 km). An electric equivalent becomes almost absurdly efficient.

We’re talking roughly 4-6 kWh per 100 kilometers (62 miles) – just a fraction of the energy consumed even by many compact electric cars. I once did the math, and a light electric motorcycle can travel 10,000 km (roughly 6,000 miles) for around $160 in electricity. Basically, your electrical bill doesn’t even notice when you own an electric motorcycle. Charging it simply doesn’t move the needle.

Instead of asking how we can fit ever-larger battery packs into increasingly larger SUVs and trucks, perhaps we should also be asking how many trips don’t need a large vehicle in the first place.

Transportation statistics across much of the developed world tell a familiar story.

Most trips involve one person. Maybe there’s also a backpack in the mix. Maybe there are some groceries getting picked up on the way home. Occasionally, there’s another passenger.

Those things are exactly what small motorcycles have been doing around the world for decades.

I recently spent some time in the Philippines, where I watched motorcycles carrying impossible-looking loads every day. Entire families would ride together. Construction materials. Furniture. Livestock. I saw two pigs on a 125cc bike, I kid you not. I’ve seen even crazier things in Thailand.

Again, I’m certainly not advocating that we adopt some of those practices in the West – there are obvious safety considerations – but it demonstrates just how incredibly capable these machines can be.

Even within normal Western expectations, a 125cc-class motorcycle is capable of handling an astonishing percentage of daily transportation needs.

This is where discussions about motorcycles often become unnecessarily polarized.

No, motorcycles aren’t ideal in every situation. Yes, heavy rain exists. Snow exists. Families with multiple children exist. Long interstate road trips exist.

Nobody is suggesting a 125cc electric motorcycle should replace every car.

If a household can replace even half of its daily driving with a lightweight electric motorcycle, that’s already a massive reduction in energy consumption, congestion, parking demand, and transportation costs.

Transportation doesn’t have to be all-or-nothing. So enough with this “but what if it rains?” stuff. Either put on a jacket that day or drive your car. But for the majority of the trips each year you take where it’s not raining, you could have done it in a much more efficient (and fun) way.

One of the biggest conversations surrounding EV adoption is charging. But smaller electric motorcycles barely participate in that problem. A 4-5 kWh battery charges overnight from an ordinary household outlet. The outlet you plug your laptop charger into is basically the equivalent of a Level 2 public charger for an e-motorcycle – that’s how fast it is.

DC fast charging isn’t really necessary on a light electric motorcycle. There’s no need for an expensive home charger. There’s no massive battery pack. Just plug it in before bed and wake up with a battery that’s been fully charged and waiting on you for hours already.

And if you want to go wild, there are swappable battery networks like Gogoro in Taiwan or Vammo in South America that can make charging unnecessary.

Another advantage rarely discussed is intimidation. Many people don’t want a 600 lb (270 kg) motorcycle producing superbike acceleration. They want something approachable, something lightweight, maneuverable, easy to park, and easy to live with.

That’s exactly why 125cc motorcycles became so successful globally.

Electric versions preserve all of those advantages while making them even easier to ride thanks to instant torque and the absence of clutch work. Many of them even come with reverse mode, making them easier to park and wiggle around even on hilly terrain.

One reason Europe has seen more progress here is that the regulatory framework already exists.

Manufacturers regularly market bikes as “125cc equivalents,” and consumers immediately understand what that means.

Licensing systems and insurance companies recognize the category. It’s a mature transportation class.

North America, by comparison, often treats motorcycles as either recreational toys or large-displacement touring machines. We’ve largely forgotten that much of the world simply sees them as transportation.

Ironically, younger riders may already be showing us the way forward.

The explosion in popularity of Sur Ron-style electric motorcycles and lightweight e-motos demonstrates that younger generations are perfectly willing to embrace two-wheeled electric transportation.

Not everyone buying those bikes is looking for motocross. Many simply enjoy the freedom, accessibility, affordability, and fun that come with traveling on two wheels.

Rather than dismissing that trend, perhaps we should recognize it as an opportunity. Today’s recreational rider often becomes tomorrow’s commuter.

If someone discovers they enjoy getting around on an electric two-wheeler, moving from a lightweight e-moto to a practical 125cc-equivalent commuter becomes a much smaller leap than convincing someone to abandon their car entirely.

One observation has stuck with me after so many years of covering the electric vehicle industry and traveling through countries where motorcycles dominate daily life. The West has spent years trying to electrify the largest, heaviest, and least efficient vehicles on our roads. Meanwhile, we’ve paid surprisingly little attention to electrifying the vehicle that already moves much of humanity every single day.

In Europe at least, there's a cliff between a pedal ebike, which anyone can ride without any pre planning, and a motorcycle which needs passing a specific test, taxing, taking out insurance and wearing safety gear. Even people with car licences need to take driving lessons and the test. It means you can't just step on a motorcycle when it makes sense you need potentially months of planning. It's much easier just to take a car you're already licensed for.

I’m not arguing that everyone should ride a motorcycle. And I’m certainly not arguing that cars no longer have an important place.

But perhaps we’ve underestimated just how many people could benefit from something in between.

Not just an electric bicycle, and not just a $25,000 electric motorcycle. Just an honest, practical, affordable electric equivalent of the vehicle that already keeps much of the world moving.

Because if we’re serious about accelerating electric transportation, maybe the future isn’t another electric pickup truck. Maybe it’s finally giving the world’s favorite motorcycle an electric motor.

#4594. In medieval Italy, a spider bite could send you into a dancing frenzy

Published Nov 10, 2026 9:01 AM EST

There’s a chance that if you visited southern Italy during the Middle Ages, you might happen upon a port town where people were dancing uncontrollably in the streets. You’d find them frantically spinning, jumping…even crawling on the ground. But unlike the broader “dancing mania” that was taking place across Europe at the same time, this dance, dubbed the “tarantella,” was more than a sickness. It was also a cure.

“Some people say that the bite of a spider caused people to tremor and shake,” Anna Harsh, a professional dancer and founder of the Allegro Dance Company, which specializes in Italian folk dances, tells Popular Science. They’d then continue moving to sweat out the poison.

Tarantism, a historical psychological and social phenomenon that led to anxiety, melancholia, and uncontrollable movement, ran rapidly throughout southern Italy from the 11th to the 17th century.

The epicenter of tarantism was Taranto, a coastal city in southern Italy’s Puglia region, which occupies the “heel” of the country’s boot shape. Each summer harvest season, local residents would spend long days working in the fields where large, hairy wolf spiders burrowed.

Most people believed that these wolf spiders carried a toxic venom. If they bit you, tarantism would quickly set in. The only cure would be to sweat out the venom through continuous, fast-paced dancing. We’re talking uncontrollable, flailing movements that would eventually exhaust both the dancer and the illness.

Although southern Italy was the epicenter of tarantism, similar outbreaks of involuntary, convulsive dancing occurred throughout the Middle Ages. The first major recorded frenzy began on June 24, 1374 in Aachen, Germany. Soon after, others followed in countries like Switzerland and modern-day France. In many of these cases, those afflicted danced uncontrollably for days or weeks. Some even died dancing. Since these events happened centuries ago, no one really knows what caused them. But the tarantism of southern Italy and its ensuing tarantella dance both seem unique.

The name “tarantula” may have originated with the wolf spiders (Lycosa tarantula) of Taranto, but wolf spiders and tarantulas belong to two entirely different spider families. Still, with a leg span that can reach up to three to four inches across, multiple sets of eyes, and a series of odd, jerky movements when they walk, wolf spiders make easy targets for conspiracy theories and urban legends.

While they can look frightening, science has determined over the years that a wolf spider’s bite is generally harmless to humans. Symptoms appear more like a mild bee sting, with a bit of localized pain and swelling, then a full-blown disco dance party. In fact, among the world’s 38,000 known spider species, only about 100 species have venom that is detrimental to humans.

In 1976, a college paper blamed the Salem witch trials on moldy bread. It wasn’t true.

Ancient Romans thought drinking gladiator blood could cure epilepsy

In medieval France, murderous pigs faced trial and execution

4 times drinking coffee was illegal—or even punishable by death

The mysterious dancing plague that killed people in 1518

The radioactive ‘miracle water’ that killed its believers

In August 1693, an anonymous Neapolitan doctor even tested the connection between the bite of a wolf spider and tarantism. He let two wolf spiders bite him in a public experiment, but the doctor never broke out into fancy footwork.

Instead, modern science shows that the extreme summer heat, physical stress, dehydration, and even ample wine drinking could have easily caused the symptoms of tarantism. Still, the wolf spider and tarantism remain undisputedly linked.

Sometimes called the “Dance of the Spider,” the tarantella began as a ritual healing dance that aimed to sweat out any venom associated with tarantism. Many versions of the tarantella exist today, though they’re more traditional folk dances than medical treatments. Instead, the  ‘tarantella as cure’ dance is more formally known as the pizzica. The word pizzica comes from the Italian verb pizzicare, which means “to pinch” or “to bite.”

“Today we might think of that ‘bite’ as something internal, like stress or anxiety,” says Harsh. Picture when someone you know suddenly loses a loved one and they’re shaking uncontrollably. “That person will dance or move and do whatever they can to help them get through that situation.”

Pizzica tarantata is performed almost like an exorcism, the spiritual practice of evicting demons or malevolent entities (such as supposed spider’s venom) through a sort of ritual—in this case, ecstatic, free-form dance.

Musicians gathered around the inflicted victim, playing incessant, fast-paced 6/8-tempo rhythms driven by a tambourine, violins, and guitars. The person suffering from tarantism would then “go into a trance,” says Harsh. “There was shaking, hopping, swirling, and turning. Some people would roll on the ground and come back up. The pizzica has movements, but you can put them in any order. It’s however the spirit moves you.”

These days, most historians and scientists agree that wolf spiders didn’t cause tarantism. Rather, tarantism was a form of mass hysteria, a situation where a group of people share the same intense fear, anxiety, or physical sickness—like dizziness, shaking, or stomach aches—even though there is no real physical or medical grounds for it.

Tarantism mostly afflicted impoverished individuals, particularly women (tarantatas). One possible reason: “Women were oppressed and faced plenty of inequality,” says Harsh. “Dance is a way that they could express themselves, even scream, through movement. That they could be the center of attention for just a minute and be seen.”

Over the centuries, the tarantella has become a celebration of life and joy rather than a frantic ritual. Italians often perform this now-beloved folk dance at weddings and festivals.

Every August, La Notte della Taranta, Europe’s largest open-air festival dedicated to traditional folk music, the pizzica, and the tarantella, takes place in Italy’s Puglia region.

Whether or not dancing works to sweat out a toxic venom, studies do show that dancing helps reduce stress and increases levels of serotonin, a hormone that helps regulate mood, sleep, and digestion.

“You know, whatever is biting at us, whether it’s grief or loss, we can move together, follow the rhythm of a drummer, and heal ourselves in a sense,” says Harsh. “The movement just takes over and we stop thinking about our troubles.”

Though if you do endure a lethal spider bite, we’d recommend the ER over two-stepping.

#4593. Low-Calorie Diet and Supervised Exercise May Reverse Early Onset Type 2 Diabetes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this new study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

The participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

The low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

In the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

This second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

At the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

“This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

Cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing issue worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

People diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

#4592. New ID. AURA is the mainstream EV VW needs – but its software is the real story

Volkswagen built its global empire on the promise of affordable, accessible transportation, embodied by the iconic Type 1 Beetle. Now facing an existential crisis after a decades-long push upmarket, the automaker faces a reckoning – and a retreat back into affordable, mass-market electric sedans like the new FAW-VW ID. AURA L5 (and the software that powers it) might be exactly what VW needs to reach a new generation of buyers.

Like the Ford Model T, the original VW Type 1 Beetle was an engineering-led answer to a basic problem: making family transportation affordable and accessible to the masses. And regardless of how you feel about Elon Musk, the Tesla Model 3 has become the spiritual successor to those cars, bringing electric transportation to millions of mainstream drivers. As the Model 3 approaches its 11th year in public view, the recently revealed all-electric ID. AURA L5 and VW JETTA looks like it could be a compelling rival to the mainstream M3.

Co-developed by Volkswagen’s Chinese and German design teams and set to be built by the FAW-VW JV, the ID. AURA L5 is an Accord/Camry-sized electric family car a practical fastback-style rear hatch, frameless doors, and a claimed “84.4% usable floor-area ratio.” The power-operated hatchback opens its maw more than 70 degrees, revealing a 39″ wide opening that can handle groceries, luggage, golf clubs, pets, bodies – whatever you got.

Don’t take my word for it, though. This is the original text from the company’s press release (translated from Chinese by Google):

The ID. AURA L5 is a pure electric family sedan, jointly designed by Chinese and German design teams, and highly replicates the design essence of the ID. AURA concept car shown at the 2025 Shanghai Auto Show. Its short overhang and long wheelbase proportions create a sleek and flowing coupe-like stance, achieving a “usable floor area ratio” of 84.4%. The sides feature true frameless doors, semi-concealed door handles, and an electric hatchback tailgate with an opening angle exceeding 70°, and an opening width exceeding 1000 mm, greatly improving the convenience of loading and unloading large items, deeply integrating fastback aesthetics with practicality. Some models will be equipped with LiDAR and feature the Hyper Sense 8 end-to-end large model, making daily travel easier and more convenient for customers.

The production version of the ID. AURA L5 is expected to pack the same 155 kW (~208 hp) electric motors announced when the concept AURA L5 was first shown last year (battery specs were not released), and was shown as part of a broader product announcement of what VW Group China would be showcasing at this year’s China International Import Expo (CIIE). These include the first two models fully equipped with Volkswagen Group’s locally developed VEGA “integrated technology matrix” (read: software), and the Volkswagen Anhui intelligent pure electric “coupe” crossover.

The announcement coincides with reports from outlets like Autocar and Reuters that Volkswagen is evaluating whether to deploy its China-developed electrical architecture across the majority of its European markets.

“According to internal discussions confirmed by Group board member and Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer,” reports Autocar’s Greg Kable, “up to 75% of the firm’s core models in Europe could eventually use the China Electronic Architecture.”

The Volkswagen Group has been struggling to deliver a software experience that resonates with customers. To their credit, they’re looking for outside help, spending billions of dollars on a software collaboration with EV startup Rivian for its upcoming electric truck brand Scout rather than going it alone. With billions of dollars and potential future of the company at stake, then, this seems like the most interesting bit of the announcement:

During the event, the immersive interactive experience exhibit “Digital Magic Cube,” which made its debut at last year’s China International Import Expo, will undergo an iterative upgrade to showcase the core strength of CEA (China Electronic Architecture), the software pillar of Volkswagen Group’s integrated self-developed technology matrix VEGA, to the attendees.

To date, CEA has enabled five new models from three joint ventures within the Volkswagen Group on a large scale, and software iterations have already been completed this year. CEA brings three core advantages to the Group’s new model lineup in China: intelligent accessibility, continuous upgrades, and safety redundancy. Through immersive interactive presentations, it provides consumers with the most intuitive experience. Empowered by the new AI R&D toolchain “C-Brain,” CEA introduces AI agents into software development, design, and engineering verification, enabling more flexible and efficient integration and innovation of vehicle intelligence capabilities, giving vehicles powerful thinking and perception abilities. Intelligent vehicles powered by CEA can better understand consumer needs, more efficiently create in-vehicle intelligent application scenarios, and better enhance digital intelligent safety redundancy, bringing Chinese consumers a new generation of intelligent mobility experience defined by Volkswagen standards

Sensible looking average car which should appeal to VW buyers provided the price, charging speed and range are right. Especially like that it has a hatch without being SUV shaped.

The show runs through November 10th, and we’ll be keeping an eye out for more details on the ID. AURA lineup and the Anhui intelligent pure electric coupe, including its powertrain, battery, and software specifications, as they become available.

#4591. Ford May Have a Replacement for the Shelby GT350 Mustang in the Works

A report citing dealer documents claim a new naturally aspirated ‘Stang will pick up where the GT350 left off.

The sixth-generation Ford Mustang Shelby GT350 was an enthusiast’s favorite. It offered a track-ready middle ground between the standard V-8-powered GT and the supercharged Shelby GT500, with a 5.2-liter naturally aspirated “Voodoo” V-8 pumping out 526 horsepower and revving to 8250 rpm, and a 6-speed manual transmission. The GT350 left production in 2020; Ford has not replaced it with a like-for-like variant for in the current seventh-generation Mustang lineup. But that could change as soon as next year.

Ford Authority is reporting that Ford sent out dealer documents confirming a new high-performance Mustang. The new Mustang would not be called the Shelby GT350—Ford has not used Shelby branding for the S650-generation Mustang, and Shelby American is currently building its own GT350. But the new model would, it seems, fulfill that role in the lineup. (Road & Track reached out to Ford for comment on the potential new Mustang, but a spokesperson only noted the brand “can’t comment on speculation” about future vehicles.)

The report claims the new Mustang would slot between the current Mustang Dark Horse and the Dark Horse SC, and would feature either a 5.2-liter or 5.4-liter naturally aspirated V-8. A six-speed manual transmission would be available, if not the only option, and the new Mustang—unlike the Dark Horse SC—would only be available as a coupe. Per the report, it would arrive in late 2027 as a 2028 model-year vehicle and have a limited production run through the 2029 model year.

Firm performance specs were not detailed for the potential new Mustang, but Ford Authority expects the power output to be around 600 hp, slotting between the 500-hp Mustang Dark Horse and the 795-hp Mustang Dark Horse SC. No word yet on pricing, either; however, the current Mustang lineup has a large gap between the $72,760 Dark Horse Premium and the $108,085 Dark Horse SC where this vehicle would fit in nicely.

Ford has been looking at options to “expand on the Mustang family,” with reported ideas including non-traditional variants such as a four-door coupe-style sedan and even an off-road variant. Reviving the manual GT350 Mustang, at least in spirit, would counter those sacrilegious notions with some welcome red meat for enthusiasts.
